mainEntity.name: Is it normal to have some exposed dentine as you get older?

acceptedAnswer.text: Some degree of enamel wear and minor gum recession can occur with age, meaning small areas of dentine exposure are not uncommon in older adults. However, "common" does not mean it should be left unaddressed. Even minor exposed dentine can progress if contributing factors — such as dietary acids, grinding, or gum disease — are not managed. A dentist can assess whether the change is age-related and stable, or whether intervention would be beneficial. It is always worthwhile raising any concerns about sensitivity or visible changes to your teeth at your routine dental check-up.

mainEntity.name: Will composite bonding completely eliminate tooth sensitivity from exposed dentine?

acceptedAnswer.text: Composite bonding may help reduce or manage sensitivity associated with exposed dentine by covering the affected surface, but it cannot be guaranteed to eliminate sensitivity entirely. Outcomes vary depending on the extent of exposure, the underlying cause, and individual patient factors. In some cases, sensitivity may improve significantly; in others, additional treatments such as desensitising agents or fluoride therapies may also be recommended. A dentist will discuss realistic expectations based on your specific clinical situation before proceeding with any treatment.

mainEntity.name: How long does composite bonding last when used to protect exposed dentine?

acceptedAnswer.text: The longevity of composite bonding varies depending on several factors, including the location of the bonded area, bite forces, dietary habits, oral hygiene practices, and whether the underlying cause of dentine exposure has been adequately managed. Composite bonding used on root surfaces or near the gumline can be subject to wear and may require maintenance or replacement over time. Your dentist will be able to give you a more specific indication based on your individual case. Regular dental review is important to monitor the condition of bonded restorations.

mainEntity.name: Can I use sensitivity toothpaste instead of getting treatment for exposed dentine?

acceptedAnswer.text: Sensitivity toothpaste containing ingredients such as potassium nitrate or stannous fluoride can help manage discomfort associated with exposed dentine and is a reasonable first-line measure for mild sensitivity. However, it does not address the underlying cause, nor does it provide physical protection for the exposed surface. If sensitivity is persistent, worsening, or affecting your daily life, a professional dental assessment is advisable. Sensitivity toothpaste may be used as part of a broader management plan alongside clinical treatment, rather than as a replacement for professional care.

mainEntity.name: Could the sensitivity I am feeling be caused by something other than exposed dentine?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes — tooth sensitivity can have several causes, including dental decay, a cracked tooth, a failing or leaking restoration, gum disease, or even referred discomfort from adjacent teeth or sinuses. This is one of the reasons why professional assessment is important. It is not possible to determine the cause of sensitivity from symptoms alone without a clinical examination, which may include X-rays and other diagnostic tools. Seeking a professional opinion helps ensure that the correct cause is identified and that the most appropriate management plan is recommended for your individual situation.

mainEntity.name: Is composite bonding a permanent solution for exposed dentine?

acceptedAnswer.text: Composite bonding is not considered a permanent solution in the same way that natural tooth structure is permanent. The material can wear, stain, or chip over time, and may require maintenance, repair, or replacement during the lifespan of the restoration. However, with good oral hygiene, appropriate diet, and regular dental review, composite bonded restorations can remain functional and aesthetically acceptable for a number of years. Managing the underlying cause of dentine exposure is particularly important to maximise the lifespan of any bonded restoration.
